traits.name: +2 Dexterity
traits.text: Ability score adjustment: +2 Dexterity. This adjustment is already included in the ability score line of this stat block.

traits.name: +1 Constitution
traits.text: Ability score adjustment: +1 Constitution. This adjustment is already included in the ability score line of this stat block.

traits.name: Arboreal Alertness
traits.text: You gain proficiency in Perception or Survival. When the check uses the sense or instinct named by this trait, add 1d4 once per short or long rest.

traits.name: Amphibious
traits.text: You can breathe air and water. You also gain a swim speed if the speed line of this stat block does not already list one.

traits.name: Poison Immunity
traits.text: You are immune to nonmagical poison and have advantage on saving throws against magical poison, unless the DM narrows this for balance.

traits.name: Poisonous Skin
traits.text: This is the Poisonous Skin ancestry feature. It grants one concrete benefit chosen from the stat block theme: proficiency in a matching skill/tool, a 1d4 bonus once per long rest to a matching check, a minor movement or sense adaptation, or a single limited magical expression if the feature is supernatural. It does not stack with another full ancestry block.

traits.name: Standing Leap
traits.text: You can use the ancestry’s quick movement once per turn or a number of times equal to your proficiency bonus per long rest, as appropriate to the trait. It helps with leaping, dashing, initiative, escaping, or moving through crowded spaces.

traits.name: Water Dependency
traits.text: You must regularly immerse yourself or remain wet according to the lineage. If you cannot, the DM may impose exhaustion or disadvantage on checks until you recover.

traits.name: Aquatic Adaptation
traits.text: You are adapted to water. You gain the swim speed, breath-holding, underwater communication, or pressure adaptation listed in this stat block. If two water traits overlap, choose one major benefit.

traits.name: Water Sense
traits.text: You can sense currents, pressure, and nearby movement in water. In water, add 1d4 to Perception or Survival checks once per short or long rest.

traits.name: Tidal Kinship
traits.text: This is the Tidal Kinship ancestry feature. It grants one concrete benefit chosen from the stat block theme: proficiency in a matching skill/tool, a 1d4 bonus once per long rest to a matching check, a minor movement or sense adaptation, or a single limited magical expression if the feature is supernatural. It does not stack with another full ancestry block.

traits.name: Bastveig's Mark
traits.text: This ancestry carries a visible or spiritual creator-god imprint. Once per long rest, add 1d4 to an ability check involving the Amphibious and Aquatic Peoples themes, a native biome, or a culture that recognizes this mark.

races.name: Dril'thar
races.description: Amphibious Mystics of the Living Waters.
extraNotes: Lore: The Dril'thar are an ancient amphibious people whose civilizations rise from swamps, flooded jungles, coral reefs, mangrove coasts, subterranean rivers, mist-choked marshes, and sacred rainforests. Across countless regions of the world, they are known as healers, navigators, mystics, hunters, survivalists, and wandering pilgrims capable of thriving where most civilizations would collapse. To outsiders, Dril'thar are often misunderstood as poisonous frogfolk, territorial swamp-creatures, or eerie marsh spirits. In truth, they are one of the most biologically adaptable and spiritually complex peoples in existence. Their philosophy teaches that all things move in cycles: rain becomes river, river becomes sea, decay becomes renewal, and death feeds life anew. Water is not merely an element to the Dril'thar—it is memory, ancestry, spirit, and destiny itself. A spawning pool may serve simultaneously as temple, cemetery, and place of prophecy, for the Dril'thar believe the currents of the world carry the echoes of those who came before.
Best Classes: Ranger Monk
races.dmHook: Use Dril'thar NPCs to show how Bastveig's single-creator doctrine appears through Amphibious and Aquatic Peoples: ancestry, culture, reputation, temptation, and divine backlash.

races.name: Tamhiogal
races.description: Aquatic Bettafolk of Hydromancy, Coral Stewardship, and Tidal Spirits.
extraNotes: Lore: Tamhiogal are aquatic beings. They resemble betta fish in their coloration, displaying vibrant shades of blues, purples, teals, and crimsons that shift with emotion and magical activity. On land, they possess scaled, graceful humanoid arms and legs, with scales rippling along their cheeks, necks, and collarbones. Their eyes are liquid and reflective, glowing faintly in dim light, and their hair consists of bioluminescent, jellyfish-like strands that can sting mildly when threatened. In water, they have gills along their necks, webbing between fingers and elbows, and fins along the spine, knees, and tail. Their legs are replaced by long, sleek caudal fins, with dorsal and anal fins enhancing maneuverability. Tamhiogal require hydration and tidal energy, which regenerate most efficiently in aquatic environments. They sustain themselves through fish, kelp, and other sea-based foods. Being immersed in water naturally maintains their hygiene and overall well-being. Exposure to polluted or stagnant water causes spiritual and emotional dissonance, while ritual bathing and communion with ocean spirits restore clarity, mood, and magical flow. Tamhiogal possess abilities attuned to both water and land. They can transition smoothly between terrestrial and aquatic forms, allowing fluid movement across both environments.
Best Classes: Druid, Cleric, Sorcerer, Bard, Ranger, Paladin, or any oceanic guardian role.
races.dmHook: Use Tamhiogal NPCs to show how Bastveig's single-creator doctrine appears through Amphibious and Aquatic Peoples: ancestry, culture, reputation, temptation, and divine backlash.

traits.name: Additional +1

traits.name: Symbiotic Assimilation

races.name: Jaspey
races.description: Ability Score Increase.
classificationNotes: Jaspey belongs in Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify because Jaspey are both animalfolk and fungal/spore folk.
extraNotes: Lore: Tiny fungal raccoon-folk born from ancient symbiotic spores and scavenger spirits, Jaspey are eerie yet lovable creatures that blur the line between woodland fae, living fungus, and grave-born scavenger. Though their appearance often resembles tiny undead raccoons stitched together with moss, mushrooms, and decay, Jaspey are fully living beings with beating hearts, warm emotions, and vibrant cultures. Standing only a few inches tall, Jaspey can sleep inside coat pockets, teacups, backpacks, hollow books, hat brims, or even small tins. Entire hidden settlements may exist unnoticed inside old walls, cemetery gardens, forgotten cupboards, abandoned wagons, or the roots of ancient trees. Jaspey are natural scavengers, herbalists, healers, thieves, potion brewers, and strange little mystics. They collect shiny objects obsessively, form strong emotional bonds with larger companions, and often travel alongside adventuring parties as medics, alchemists, scouts, or magical nuisances.
races.dmHook: Use Jaspey NPCs to show how Nephthysra's single-creator doctrine appears through Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify Races: ancestry, culture, reputation, temptation, and divine backlash.

classificationNotes: Aburata belongs in Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify because it crosses fiendish planar ancestry with equine-bodied traits.
extraNotes: Lore: The Aburatas are a race of infernal beings . They possess two distinct forms that reflect their dual nature: a humanoid form and a quadrupedal, equine-inspired form. In humanoid form, Aburatas have polished, taut skin resembling obsidian, molten iron, or amethyst-violet, often etched with glowing sigils or ember-like vein patterns that pulse with their emotions. Their eyes blaze with infernal fire or sink into abyssal voids, and their hair can range from jet black to flame-red, silver-violet, or stark white. Horns emerge in unique shapes such as spiraled, antlered, or blade-like, glowing faintly with infernal energy, while a prehensile tail flickers with embers or faint hellfire, aiding balance and expressive gestures. In quadrupedal form, their humanoid upper bodies transition into powerful horse-like torsos sheathed in scaled textures reminiscent of volcanic stone or blackened steel, with muscular limbs ending in broad hooves that leave glowing, smoldering prints. The tail grows longer and more expressive, capable of grasping objects or assisting in movements, while the air around them carries heat and shadow, enhancing their imposing presence. Their voices are resonant and hypnotic, capable of commanding attention or inspiring unease. Aburatas are sustained by infernal energy rather than ordinary nourishment, drawing vitality from places of power, fire-lit areas, or sites infused with dark influence. They maintain stamina, focus, and resilience through sheer will and magical energy, and their infernal heritage grants them natural resistance to fire, curses, and corruption. Aburatas are highly charismatic, their presence amplifying social influence, persuasion, and intimidation. They exhibit keen dexterity and precision in both combat and manipulation of objects, aided by sharp, clawed hands in humanoid form.
Best Classes: Warlock, Paladin, Bard, Sorcerer, Fighter, Rogue, or any charismatic commander role.
races.dmHook: Use Aburata NPCs to show how Nephthysra's single-creator doctrine appears through Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify Races: ancestry, culture, reputation, temptation, and divine backlash.

races.name: Volsarii
races.description: Four-Armed Ferriers of Souls, Liminal Balance, and Ethereal Wings.
classificationNotes: Volsarii belongs in Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify because it crosses liminal, soul-ferrying, winged, and multi-limbed traits.
extraNotes: Lore: Volsariis are ethereal, multi-limbed beings . They possess four arms as a standard trait, elongated ears that curve upward and nearly resemble horns, and long, sensitive antennae atop their heads that detect changes in the environment, subtle emotions, and spiritual currents. Their skin ranges widely from iridescent shades of deep blues, greens, and storm-gray to luminous pastels, dawn-pinks, or shadowed violets, often streaked or veined with faint magical light, and may carry subtle markings that glow or shift with emotion, spiritual energy, or ambient magic. Their eyes vary from softly glowing gold, silver, and sky-blue to hollow voids, nebula-like patterns, or luminous starlight, reflecting both perception of the physical world and awareness of spirits, dream energy, or hidden currents. Hair flows lightly or appears almost weightless, with colors spanning metallic, pastel, starlit, or shadowed hues, sometimes giving the impression of liquid light, drifting mist, or feather-like strands. They maintain an elegant, deliberate grace in movement, capable of silent terrestrial motion, climbing, gliding, or, in their final life cycle, sprouting vast wings ranging from feathered to gossamer or ethereal forms, allowing them flight and aerial control that expresses both power and precision. Volsariis act as ferriers of the dead for Nyxarion, guiding souls through liminal spaces and maintaining the balance between life and death. They are attuned to both the waking and spiritual realms, able to sense, communicate with, and influence spirits, manage transitions, and preserve memory through subtle manipulation of energy, aura, or pheromones. Their abilities blend ethereal perception, dream- or shadow-influenced magic, and radiant or elemental powers, allowing them to phase through matter, weave illusions, manipulate light, wind, or celestial energies, and project calming, inspiring, or disorienting auras. Rituals, meditation, and communion with sacred or magical sites restore vitality, while harsh, chaotic, or energy-depleted environments can diminish focus and magical resonance. Volsariis draw sustenance primarily from ambient magic, spiritual energy, or dream currents rather than conventional food, though symbolic consumption may accompany ceremonial practices. Their culture emphasizes cycles, reflection, guardianship, guidance, and balance, blending artistic expression, dreamwork, and ritual observances with precise attention to the flow of life, death, and magical currents.
Best Classes: Cleric, Paladin, Warlock, Bard, Monk, Wizard, or any psychopomp/guardian role.

races.name: Deorbasun
races.description: Majestic Beast-Souled Guardians of Instinct, Honor, and Mystical Territory.
classificationNotes: Deorbasun belongs in Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify because it crosses animal, guardian, mystical, and soul-animal traits.
extraNotes: Lore: Deorbasuns are majestic. Their physiques range from muscular, feline-like frames to lithe, agile forms with fur, scales, or earth-toned skin, reflecting a deep connection to predatory grace, wilderness instinct, and mystical energy. Heights vary widely, from six to nine feet, and their limbs are long and flexible, ending in retractable claws or talons capable of channeling energy or venom. Eyes glow with intelligence and authority, displaying hues from ember and gold to crystalline blues, greens, or silver, and often carry faint luminescence that responds to magic or emotion. Hair and manes vary from obsidian black, smoldering crimson, and radiant gold to bioluminescent strands, shimmered locks, or ethereal highlights, often adorned with beads, feathers, bones, or gemstones marking achievements, lineage, or ritual significance. Wings, tails, or subtle soul-animal traits enhance both presence and ability, with wings capable of flight or generating gusts, tails delivering venom, radiant energy, or prehensile utility, and faint ethereal markings or patterns tying form to instinct and magic. Deorbasuns possess extraordinary physical and magical abilities that blend predatory skill, shapeshifting versatility, and environmental attunement. They can leap with precision, maneuver through air or terrain with grace, and strike with claws, fangs, or tails imbued with energy or venom. Some can shift subtly to reflect traits of a soul-animal, such as enhanced senses, agility, or elemental affinities, while others maintain a consistently imposing, feline-like or beastly form. Their endurance and stamina are exceptional, allowing them to traverse rugged terrain, hunt, or perform ritualized movement for extended periods. They absorb energy through magical currents, prey, or ambient mana, and their focus and vitality are renewed through hunting, meditation, ritual exposure, or communion with natural and mystical environments. Deorbasuns are highly perceptive, capable of reading subtle environmental cues, sensing magical disturbances, and coordinating with wildlife or allies in ways that reflect both strategic intelligence and instinctual response.
Best Classes: Barbarian, Fighter, Ranger, Druid, Paladin, Monk, or any guardian/hunter role.
races.dmHook: Use Deorbasun NPCs to show how Nephthysra's single-creator doctrine appears through Miscellaneous and Hard-to-Classify Races: ancestry, culture, reputation, temptation, and divine backlash.

worldFrame.text: The public hymns remember creation as blessing. The older ledgers record appetite, design, bloodline, body, and use with colder handwriting.

mixed_heritage_full_package_import.usage: Mixed Heritage is a separate dropdown from racial bloodlines / lineages. It never replaces the racial bloodline menu. Each mixed-heritage record contains its complete in-book recommended stat block.
normalizationNotes: Genasi is now a parent race with Air, Earth, Fire, and Water Genasi as bloodlines/lineages.
Panolima remains a parent race with Earth, Fire, Water, Air, and Aether Panolima bloodlines/lineages.
Umbral Human, Deep Gnome, Shadow Goblin, Lorwyn Changeling, Githyanki, and Githzerai were moved from standalone pages into parent-race lineage dropdowns where appropriate.
Mixed heritage records for moved lineages now appear under the parent race pages.
All x-born standalone entries in this package were converted into parent-race dropdown structures, including Curse-Born, Death-Born, Energy-Born, Relic-Born, Web-Born, Nature-Born, and Shadow-Born.
Energy-Born now contains Ashborn, Azureborn, Bogborn, Deepborn, Flamekin, Rimekin, Snowborn, and Stoneborn as dropdown lineages.
Faerie, Fairy, and Gandirosha are now lineages under the Fey-Folk parent race page.
Mixed heritage dropdown records for moved entries now appear on their new parent race pages and preserve the former standalone race as the lineage name.
The open-book spread keeps the 668×1047 page proportions per page.
Final audit pass aligned the HTML book with the DOCX package category structure while preserving user-requested parent-race dropdowns.
Bloodlines and lineages are treated as the same selector type throughout the book: Bloodline / Lineage.
Dwarf now includes Hill Dwarf, Mountain Dwarf, and Duergar as bloodline / lineage options.
Gnome now includes Forest Gnome, Rock Gnome, and Deep Gnome as bloodline / lineage options.
Halfling now includes Lightfoot Halfling, Stout Halfling, and Ghostwise Halfling as bloodline / lineage options.
Goblin now contains Goblin, Hobgoblin, Bugbear, Gobboc, Shadow Goblin, Boggart, and Verdan as bloodline / lineage options; the moved goblinoids are no longer loose standalone pages.
Tiefling now includes Infernal Tiefling, Abyssal Tiefling, and Feral as bloodline / lineage options.
Shifter now includes Beasthide, Longtooth, Swiftstride, and Wildhunt Shifter as bloodline / lineage options.
All race pages, bloodline / lineage options, and all 7,550 mixed-heritage records have stat blocks.

axes.Lawfulness: Chaotic ↔ Lawful; relationship to structure, rules, duty, and rebellion.

alignment_reference_from_race_package.scale: Each axis runs 0–3000; 1500 is true neutral; 250 points moves one tracked position.
alignment_reference_from_race_package.profileNameRule: Official guide names are used where listed. Neutral-altruism profiles with Lawful or Chaotic lawfulness are named by extending the guide’s neutral suffix pattern so every race, lineage, and mixed heritage has a readable profile.

paragraphs: The Imprisoned Gods of Belavadös
God-by-God Creator Compendium
Temple record of divine domains, created peoples, manifestations, and sacred histories
God Index
Organized in the official 1-22 pantheon order, with each entry indexed by god name.
Pantheon Overview: The Imprisoned Gods of Belavadös

The beings known as the Gods are not divine in any benevolent sense of the word. They are not protectors, moral guides, or loving creators. They are ancient predators who shaped the peoples of Belavadös from their own designs, cultivating mortal life not out of compassion, but fascination, utility, hunger, and dominion. Every race in the world traces its origin to one of these entities. Humanity and all their neighboring bloodlines, the elves, dwarves, beastfolk, dragons, constructs, shadow-born peoples, and stranger things still all exist because the Gods desired them to.
For most of history, the Gods ruled openly.
Their reign ended only a few generations ago.

There are still elders alive who remember when the Gods walked freely through cities. There are rulers whose grandparents once knelt before them in person. Ancient temples still stand in active use. Some noble bloodlines carry marks and blessings granted directly by the Gods themselves. The scars of divine rule are recent enough that the world has not fully recovered from it.
The imprisonment of the Gods was not born from heroism alone.

The great courts, empires, magocracies, and royal houses of the world eventually united against them after centuries of exploitation, feeding, wars, and manipulation. Entire civilizations had become dependent upon the Gods’ touch and the substances derived from them. Kingdoms rose and collapsed according to divine appetites. The Gods cultivated worship through addiction, fear, ecstasy, and dependency until much of the world could no longer distinguish faith from enslavement.
Yet even when the rulers of Belavadös rebelled, they did not destroy the Gods.
They could have tried.
Instead, they chose imprisonment.
The decision was deliberate, political, and deeply corrupt.
The Gods were too useful.

Their blood, called ichor, had become woven into every powerful institution on the continent. Ichor could heal disease, strengthen magic, extend life, fuel rituals, empower curses, create poisons, alter minds, and sustain entire industries of alchemy and sorcery. Fresh ichor could be consumed directly for euphoric visions and temporary supernatural gifts. When dried and refined into black crystalline powder, it became one of the most valuable substances in existence.
Entire economies depended upon it.
The rulers of the world did not wish to free their people from the Gods completely. They wanted control over them.
So the great prisons were built.

Across Belavadös, hidden beneath palaces, oceans, mountains, cathedrals, and sealed vault-cities, the Gods remain confined within colossal arcane prisons maintained by generations of royal bloodlines, mage orders, and secretive courts. These prisons are not simple cages. They are feeding engines and suppression systems designed specifically to keep the Gods alive, weakened, and harvestable.
The prisons force limitations upon them.

The Gods are still allowed to feed, because starvation would eventually drive them feral and uncontrollable. However, the enchantments binding them prevent them from fully killing during the feeding process. The prisons interrupt the final stages of consumption, forcibly cutting the Gods off before death can occur. This leaves them trapped in a permanent state of weakness and hunger, never fully satisfied, never strong enough to break free entirely.
Many believe this endless starvation has made them crueler than they were during their reign.

Prisoners, criminals, political enemies, debtors, cultists, and volunteers are regularly brought into the feeding chambers beneath powerful cities. Some are sacrificed unwillingly. Others enter willingly in exchange for wealth, status, miracles, or ichor. Entire black markets exist around feeding rights and divine exposure. Noble houses secretly compete for access to stronger concentrations of ichor harvested from particular Gods.
The public is taught that the prisons protect civilization.
The truth is that civilization has merely transformed divine predation into an industry.
The Gods themselves appear almost human.

At first glance, they resemble impossibly tall and unnervingly beautiful mortals draped in layered robes, dark ceremonial fabrics, and armor-like organic growths that seem half-grown from their flesh. Their proportions are subtly wrong. Their limbs are fractionally too long. Their fingers bend with unnatural fluidity. Their eyes linger too still. Their smiles hold expressions a heartbeat too late. Every feature evokes the uncanny sensation of something attempting to imitate humanity without fully understanding it.

Their skin possesses a pale translucence beneath which black ichor pulses slowly through vein-like channels. Their voices sound layered, as though several tones speak at once beneath the surface of ordinary speech. Their movements are smooth enough to feel predatory even while standing motionless.
To devoted followers, the Gods usually feed through their hands.

Embedded within each palm lies a feeding organ concealed beneath smooth flesh. When feeding begins, the palm opens like layered petals, revealing black tendrils and sensory filaments that pierce both flesh and spirit simultaneously. The God presses its hand against the chest, throat, face, or heart of the victim while drawing life force directly from the soul itself.

For loyal worshippers, favored servants, and willing thralls, this process is intimate, euphoric, and strangely gentle despite the horror of it. The Gods deliberately preserve beauty in these moments because devotion enriches the feeding experience. Their followers often describe feelings of warmth, transcendence, emotional release, and overwhelming closeness during feeding. Many become addicted after only a single encounter.
But the Gods are not kind creatures.
When feeding upon enemies, strangers, or victims they wish to terrify, they abandon the illusion of refinement entirely.
Their bodies unfold into something monstrous.

Mouths split open across their flesh in impossible numbers. Jaws emerge along their arms, ribs, throats, torsos, and faces. Teeth blossom beneath the skin like flowers of bone. Entire sections of their bodies peel apart into feeding maws lined with black tendrils and wet sensory organs. Their limbs distort and elongate while mouths speak, scream, laugh, and feed simultaneously.
Some Gods enjoy horrifying their victims before feeding. Others consider it entertainment. A few see it as honesty, stripping away the false human shape to remind mortals what stands before them.
The prisons suppress much of this transformation, but never fully.
Those who work within the feeding chambers often report hearing wet breathing behind walls, whispers emerging from sealed stone, or the sound of mouths chewing despite no visible source.
The ichor produced by the Gods is among the most coveted substances in existence.

Fresh ichor appears as thick black fluid with an oily sheen that reflects light incorrectly. It remains warm regardless of temperature and moves slightly on its own when exposed to living flesh. Consuming it can produce visions, magical enhancement, heightened perception, prophetic dreams, or horrifying mutations depending upon purity and dosage.
Dried ichor becomes a fine black powder used in countless applications.
Spell catalysts and magical amplifiers.
Necromantic rituals.
Healing tonics and regenerative medicine.
Addictive narcotics.
Ritual poisons.
Cursecraft.
Longevity treatments.
Divine communion rites.
Psychic enhancement.
Biological experimentation.
The most powerful courts guard their ichor reserves more fiercely than gold.
Entire wars have nearly begun over access to imprisoned Gods.

Despite their imprisonment, the Gods remain dangerously influential. Their whispers still reach beyond their prisons through dreams, visions, cults, and psychic resonance. Some maintain devoted followings numbering in the thousands. Others secretly manipulate noble bloodlines or criminal organizations from within confinement. A few appear genuinely amused by the current arrangement, seeing mortals’ attempts at control as merely another stage in the relationship between predator and prey.
The world of Belavadös now exists in an uneasy balance.
Civilization fears the Gods.
Civilization depends upon the Gods.
And beneath the great cities of the world, the creators of every living race remain hungry, half-starved, and very much alive.
Belavadös Race Families and Their Creator Gods

These final race families are recorded here before the god-by-god sections for ease of reference. The language is temple-formal on the surface, but the classification logic beneath it is deliberately colder: families, bloodlines, and habitats arranged as divine inventory rather than affection.
God-by-God Compendium
Each section records the god's domains, creator category, created peoples, manifestation, and sacred histories.
1. Nebyrr
Created Belavadös People(s)

Nebyrr is now recorded as the single creator-god of Humans, Near-Humans, and Mixed Heritage: Human, Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Half-Orc (Human + Orc Lineage), Khoravar Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Umbral Human. The public hymn calls this lineage and blessing; the older register reads like curated divine husbandry, sorting bodies, habitats, temperaments, and spirit-resonance so civilization, lineage, dynasties, marriage, inheritance, and social order never depends on one mortal pattern alone.
Created Peoples and Bloodlines
Manifestation / Appearance

Nebyrr appears as a towering noble figure with soft features that never blink at the correct time. Their skin resembles polished ivory stretched over moving shadows. Their hands are delicate and warm during feeding, often cradling the face or chest of favored followers like a lover or parent.
Condensed Creator Summary

Under the final compendium, Nebyrr's racial domain is Humans, Near-Humans, and Mixed Heritage. It contains Human, Umbral Human, Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Khoravar Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Half-Orc (Human + Orc Lineage), Half-Elf - High Elf, Half-Elf - Wood Elf, Half-Elf - Drow (Underdark), Half-Elf - Eladrin, Half-Elf - Astral Elf, Half-Elf - Sea Elf, Half-Elf - Shadar-Kai, Half-Elf - Pallid Elf, Half-Elf - Star Elf (Lunar/Heavenly), Half-Elf - Avariel (Winged), Half-Elf - Snow Elf (Frostbound), Half-Elf - Sun Elf, Half-Elf - Moon Elf, Half-Elf - Shadowmoor Elf, Half-Elf - Celestial Elf, Half-Elf - Kaluseban, Khoravar - High Elf, Khoravar - Wood Elf, Khoravar - Drow (Underdark), Khoravar - Eladrin, Khoravar - Astral Elf, and 11 more. These lineages are presented to mortals as sacred variety, culture, inheritance, and survival; the older temple accounting makes the design feel colder, as if each people was tuned to a different habitat, lifespan, fear, longing, loyalty, body, and resonance before being released into the world.
Expanded Pantheon Lore

Within the Belavadösian pantheon, Nebyrr is not merely a goddess of marriage but a sovereign architect of divine legitimacy, sacred union, and enforced order within a court sustained by consumption. As queen consort to one of the High Fathers of Heaven, she holds immense ceremonial authority within the gilded and obsidian hierarchy of the celestial court, where devotion and terror are indistinguishable. Her presence is described as impeccably regal and inhumanly perfect, embodying the classical Belavadös ideal of divinity as luminous, symmetrical, and untouched by decay. Her crown is both symbol and sigil, marking her as wife, regulator, and enforcer of sanctioned dominion within the predatory order of the gods.

Final race-compendium doctrine: Nebyrr holds this whole family through civilization, lineage, dynasties, marriage, inheritance, and social order. The canon list includes Human, Umbral Human, Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Khoravar Half-Elf (choose an Elf Bloodline), Half-Orc (Human + Orc Lineage), Half-Elf - High Elf, Half-Elf - Wood Elf, Half-Elf - Drow (Underdark), Half-Elf - Eladrin, Half-Elf - Astral Elf, Half-Elf - Sea Elf, Half-Elf - Shadar-Kai, Half-Elf - Pallid Elf, Half-Elf - Star Elf (Lunar/Heavenly), Half-Elf - Avariel (Winged), Half-Elf - Snow Elf (Frostbound), Half-Elf - Sun Elf, Half-Elf - Moon Elf, and 19 more. Temple language preserves reverence, but its colder margins classify each race and bloodline by yield, pressure, environment, devotion, fear, beauty, endurance, and the particular note it awakens in the god's appetite. This revision preserves the deity's domains, manifestation, mythology, imprisoning context, and sacred-history material around it; only the racial classification has been replaced to match the current compendium.

Nebyrr’s personality is defined by pride and calculated intelligence, yet within Belavadös myth this pride is inseparable from the brutal administrative logic of the pantheon. Her jealousy is not emotional in a mortal sense but territorial and systemic, directed toward any mortal devotion, sacrificial offering, or divine favor that bypasses her authority. Such transgressions are interpreted as violations of sacred structure itself. When Valkhamesh extends attention toward mortal consorts, Nebyrr’s wrath manifests not as simple vengeance but as metaphysical correction, restructuring fates, collapsing bloodlines, and redirecting sacrificial cycles to restore what she perceives as proper order. Figures such as Io, Semele, and Leto become focal points of divine redistribution, where mortal suffering is not incidental but absorbed into the larger economy of celestial consumption.

Despite her severity, Nebyrr remains one of the primary embodiments of sanctified union within the pantheon. Marriage under her domain is not sentimental but binding law, a metaphysical contract governing the distribution of divine essence, mortal tribute, and inherited obligation. Weddings blessed by her authority are inseparable from future sacrificial consequence, ensuring families remain integrated into the divine feeding cycle across generations. Her relationship with Valkhamesh reflects the fractured unity of the High Fathers’ court, where Valkhamesh governs expansion, dominion, and divine projection, while Nebyrr governs legitimacy, continuity, and structural enforcement. Their dynamic is both intimate and adversarial, shaped by competing necessities within a system that survives on regulated hunger rather than harmony.

In Belavadös myth, Nebyrr’s pursuit of Nebyrrcles is not framed as petty vengeance but as a prolonged confrontation with unstable divine inheritance. Nebyrrcles represents an anomaly within the system, a mortal shaped vessel saturated with stolen divinity, repeatedly surviving sacrificial collapse and resisting the expected cycles of consumption. Nebyrr’s attempts to contain him are interpreted as correction rather than punishment, an effort to force irregular divinity back into structured order. His eventual ascension is not a defeat of Nebyrr but a systemic compromise, where contradiction is absorbed rather than eliminated, revealing the limits of even divine regulation.

Above and surrounding Nebyrr’s domain stands the broader pantheon of Belavadös, where gods such as Valkhamesh, Horundar, Nefarokir, Raeshkul, Enkirael, Sokhivar, Sigrananna, Thalunesh, Ishtanora, Asethyr, Marduthor, Hathruna, Nephthysra, Freyseth, Oskar'enlil, Eirzunet, Anubaldir, Setrimir, Iskareth, and the imprisoned Colossus Thoryn-Rahek each embody distinct forms of predation, order, and metaphysical function. None are sustained by faith alone. Every prayer, sacrifice, and act of devotion carries fragments of mortal essence upward, feeding divine existence. Temples are not places of worship but engines of sustenance, clerics unknowingly surrendering portions of their spirit through ritual, while warlocks create direct conduits of emotional consumption through pact-bound suffering, desire, ambition, and pain. Civilization unknowingly grows around this system, mistaking divine consumption for sacred balance.

As knowledge spreads across Belavadös, the truth of this system becomes increasingly difficult to conceal. Industrial expansion, population growth, and global conflict amplify the emotional and spiritual output of mortals, intensifying divine hunger rather than satisfying it. Entire economies, wars, and political systems are subtly shaped to sustain the pantheon’s feeding cycle. Beneath even the gods’ awareness lies the ancient fear of Thoryn-Rahek, the first great hunger, sealed after the Colossus Wars in which entire civilizations, seas, and mountains were consumed by primordial ruin. The gods’ victory over Thoryn-Rahek did not end fear, but transformed it into insatiable dependence, as immortality became inseparable from consumption.

Roughly four centuries ago, a coordinated rebellion spanning nations, secret orders, arcane institutions, industrial coalitions, and disillusioned clergy united against the gods. Massive metaphysical vault prisons were constructed across Belavadös, binding each deity within a sealed prison realm designed not to kill but to restrict divine consumption through catastrophic feedback systems. Each of the twenty-one seals corresponds to a specific god, inflicting unbearable agony whenever excessive sustenance is drawn from mortal worship. Though imprisoned, the gods remain active, granting limited miracles, visions, and controlled divine interaction, but always under restriction.

In the modern age, Belavadös exists in a state of regulated dependence. Skyships run on contained divine energy, rail systems are protected by consecrated wards, and portal networks rely on stabilized celestial resonance. Governments strictly regulate worship through licensed temples, controlled prayer quotas, and monitored clerical systems. Illegal cults are hunted by inquisitorial agencies and peacekeeping forces, while sanctioned faith is treated as both resource and risk. Civilization believes it has escaped divine domination, yet it continues to survive through carefully rationed divinity extracted from the very beings it imprisoned.

Even within confinement, the gods continue to influence the world. Valkhamesh rages within his stormbound prison, Horundar haunts sailors with visions of drowning worlds, Enkirael feeds upon warfare and fear across battlefields, Asethyr spreads madness through hidden revelries, Freyseth instructs forbidden magic in secret covens, and Nefarokir waits with patient inevitability beneath creation. Raeshkul increasingly questions whether humanity’s victory represents justice or imbalance, as mortal civilization replicates the same patterns of control, exploitation, and consumption that defined the gods themselves.

The seals binding the pantheon are not purely physical but metaphysical structures weakened by suffering, corruption, betrayal, and collapse. Every act of cruelty, addiction, and despair fractures the prison system that holds the gods at bay. Secret cults dedicated to individual deities and to Thoryn-Rahek himself work toward the unraveling of these seals, believing that release will restore balance or bring inevitable renewal. Prophecy warns that when the Final Seal breaks and Thoryn-Rahek returns, the gods will face an impossible choice between alliance with humanity or renewed consumption of it to survive the Devourer beneath creation.

At the core of Belavadös lies a contradiction sustained by Nebyrr’s foundational influence and the broader divine order she helped define. Civilization is built upon lineage, marriage, inheritance, and structured identity, yet it survives only through the same systems of regulated divine consumption that imprison its creators. The gods are neither purely evil nor innocent, but ancient forces bound by hunger and restriction. Mortals are neither free nor enslaved, but dependent participants in a system they both rejected and rebuilt. Beneath it all remains the slow erosion of trust, morality, and stability, where apocalypse is not an event but a gradual unraveling of every structure that holds the world, including the divine order Nebyrr once forged to preserve it.
2. Sigrananna
Created Belavadös People(s)
Created Peoples and Bloodlines

Sigrananna is now recorded as the single creator-god of Elf Parent Race and Elf Bloodlines: Elf. The public hymn calls this lineage and blessing; the older register reads like curated divine husbandry, sorting bodies, habitats, temperaments, and spirit-resonance so forests, moonlight, wilderness, graceful hunters, elven beauty, and inherited elven bloodlines never depends on one mortal pattern alone.
Sigrananna appears ethereal, with silver-black hair flowing as though underwater, and a smile that reveals too many teeth when closely observed.
Condensed Creator Summary

Under the final compendium, Sigrananna's racial domain is Elf Parent Race and Elf Bloodlines. It contains Elf, High Elf, Wood Elf, Drow (Underdark), Eladrin, Astral Elf, Sea Elf, Shadar-Kai, Pallid Elf, Star Elf (Lunar/Heavenly), Avariel (Winged), Snow Elf (Frostbound), Sun Elf, Moon Elf, Shadowmoor Elf, Celestial Elf, Kaluseban. These lineages are presented to mortals as sacred variety, culture, inheritance, and survival; the older temple accounting makes the design feel colder, as if each people was tuned to a different habitat, lifespan, fear, longing, loyalty, body, and resonance before being released into the world.
Expanded Pantheon Lore

Within the Belavadösian interpretation of the pantheon, Sigrananna is not merely the goddess of the hunt and wilderness, but a celestial predator bound to the sacred cycle of vitality and depletion. She embodies untamed nature in its most merciless expression, where forests do not simply shelter life but consume and reclaim it in equal measure. As a twin of Sokhivar and daughter of Valkhamesh and Leto, she occupies a liminal position within divine aristocracy, respected and feared in equal measure, never fully controlled even by the High Fathers of Heaven. Among all divine forces, she is regarded as the most precise embodiment of natural law made sentient, governing thresholds where life begins, where it is taken, and where it returns to the wild order that predates civilization.

Sigrananna’s domain extends across wilderness, moonlight, animals, and childbirth, all of which reflect controlled transitions rather than static states of existence. In Belavadös myth, her famed independence is understood not as simple refusal of divine matrimony, but as an absolute rejection of being bound to the broader hierarchical hunger of the pantheon. She does not consume through excess or indulgence like many other gods, but through measured necessity. Her hunts are deliberate and sparse, always framed as restoration of balance rather than conquest. To her worshipers, she is neither merciful nor cruel in human terms, but instead an inevitability that determines when life is allowed to flourish and when it must be returned to the cycle of the wild.

Final race-compendium doctrine: Sigrananna holds this whole family through forests, moonlight, wilderness, graceful hunters, elven beauty, and inherited elven bloodlines. The canon list includes Elf, High Elf, Wood Elf, Drow (Underdark), Eladrin, Astral Elf, Sea Elf, Shadar-Kai, Pallid Elf, Star Elf (Lunar/Heavenly), Avariel (Winged), Snow Elf (Frostbound), Sun Elf, Moon Elf, Shadowmoor Elf, Celestial Elf, Kaluseban. Temple language preserves reverence, but its colder margins classify each race and bloodline by yield, pressure, environment, devotion, fear, beauty, endurance, and the particular note it awakens in the god's appetite. This revision preserves the deity's domains, manifestation, mythology, imprisoning context, and sacred-history material around it; only the racial classification has been replaced to match the current compendium.

The Sea Elf are born from her reach into tidal wilderness, where ocean and shoreline become living thresholds between worlds, carrying her presence into abyssal forests and coral sanctuaries. The Shadowmoor Elf emerge from regions where sunlight is fractured through dense canopy and corrupted wilds, embodying survival within environments where nature itself has become unpredictable and dangerous. The Shadar-Kai represent the most distant echo of Sigrananna’ influence, shaped by the boundary between life and death, existing in liminal shadow states where endurance replaces flourishing, and survival becomes its own form of devotion to the cycle she governs.

Across Belavadös, Sigrananna is interpreted differently from most of the pantheon because she does not participate in the same economies of divine consumption that define the High Fathers. While gods like Valkhamesh, Horundar, and Enkirael feed upon worship, fear, and suffering in vast uncontrolled cycles, Sigrananna is said to “hunt sparingly,” taking only what is necessary to maintain equilibrium within her domains. This restraint positions her as both anomaly and stabilizing force within a pantheon otherwise defined by insatiable appetite. Her association with childbirth reinforces this duality, as she is both the guardian of arrival into existence and the silent presence at its departure.

Her most infamous myth, the fate of Actaeon, is interpreted in Belavadös scripture as a ritual unraveling rather than simple punishment. When Actaeon witnesses her in a forbidden moment, Sigrananna does not merely transform him into a stag, but strips away his human essence entirely, dispersing it into the wilderness itself. What remains becomes a creature defined by instinct rather than identity, ultimately consumed by his own hunting hounds in a perfect loop of natural consequence. Similarly, when Niobe defies divine order through pride in mortal lineage, Sigrananna and Sokhivar enact a coordinated culling of her offspring, framed not as cruelty but as the reclamation of lives that had exceeded their ordained measure within the balance of existence.

Even within a pantheon defined by hunger, Sigrananna remains an anomaly. Valkhamesh respects her authority but cannot fully integrate her into his systems of divine control. Sokhivar shares a bond of twin opposition with her, where light and hunt, prophecy and instinct, order and wilderness exist in constant philosophical tension. Among the gods, she is often described as the edge of the forest where even divinity hesitates to step further, a boundary where control gives way to inevitability. She embodies freedom not as innocence, but as sovereign authority over the terms by which life is taken and returned.

Long before the rail empires stretched across Belavadös, before skyships carved luminous paths through stormlit skies, and before regulated portals bound distant regions through controlled arcane systems, the world belonged entirely to the gods. The Belavadösian pantheon ruled openly as immortal sovereigns, each sustained not by faith alone but by consumption of mortal essence embedded in worship, sacrifice, emotion, and devotion. Temples functioned as both sanctuaries and engines of divine sustenance, feeding the gods through structured reverence that civilizations accepted as natural law.

As mortal civilizations advanced, they began uncovering the truth that divine power was not passive blessing but systemic consumption. The rise of industry intensified this imbalance, as growing populations and sprawling cities became vast reservoirs of emotional and spiritual energy. Wars were subtly influenced, economies shaped, and suffering perpetuated because all of it fed the pantheon. Even the gods themselves became aware that their immortality depended upon an increasingly unstable dependency, one that would eventually lead to collapse or rebellion.

Beneath this system lay an older horror. Thoryn-Rahek, the ancient Colossus king and devourer beneath creation, remained imprisoned after the Colossus Wars that nearly erased existence itself. From that war, the gods inherited not only victory but fear, and from fear, insatiable hunger. They learned that immortality was not stability, but dependence upon continuous consumption. This realization shaped their dominion and deepened their need for mortal essence.

Roughly four centuries before the present age, the greatest powers of Belavadös united in secret against the pantheon. Industrial republics, royal bloodlines, arcane orders, railway magnates, naval coalitions, druidic circles, and disillusioned clerics collaborated to construct a system capable of imprisoning divinity itself. Across the continent, massive vault-prisons were forged beneath mountains, oceans, deserts, forests, and forgotten ruins. These were not cages of stone, but metaphysical engines bound by arcane law, industrial machinery, sacrificial contracts, and Colossus-forged restraint.

Twenty-one seals were created, each binding a specific deity within a controlled prison-realm. These seals did not destroy the gods, for divinity could not be easily killed, but they restricted their ability to feed. Whenever a god attempted excessive consumption, the seals inflicted catastrophic feedback that tore through their essence in unbearable agony. For the first time in existence, the gods could starve without dying, and thus began the Age of Containment.

Despite their imprisonment, the gods remain active within Belavadös. They still answer prayers, empower warlocks, and influence dreams, but only through heavily regulated systems of worship controlled by governments and sanctioned institutions. Skyships, portal networks, and rail systems all rely upon carefully rationed divine energy, creating a civilization that has freed itself from divine domination while simultaneously becoming dependent upon its remnants.

Sigrananna remains one of the most stable and least destabilizing forces within this imprisoned pantheon. While other gods rage, manipulate, or fracture reality in response to starvation, she continues her measured cycle of hunt and restraint. Her wilderness endures not as a domain of chaos, but as a system of balance that neither civilization nor divine hunger can fully corrupt. Yet even she understands that balance is not permanence, and that every seal, every act of corruption, and every collapse of moral order brings the pantheon closer to the moment when restraint can no longer hold.

In Belavadös, the ultimate horror is not sudden destruction, but gradual unraveling. Civilization depends upon controlled divinity, the gods depend upon constrained hunger, and mortals exist between both systems as both sustenance and architect. Sigrananna stands at the threshold of that contradiction, the eternal hunter who does not simply take life, but decides whether the cycle itself continues to hold.
3. Marduthor

In the current age of Belavadös, humanity lives within a paradoxical stability. Marduthor endures at the center of this contradiction, the architect of systems that both empower mortal independence and sustain divine dependency. Ishtanora’s response is not only maternal anguish but systemic withdrawal, a refusal to maintain the agricultural flow that sustains the surface world. In her grief, fields fail, ecosystems falter, and mortal civilizations wither, not as punishment but as the inevitable consequence of severed divine regulation within an interconnected system of consumption and dependency.

This collapse is remembered as one of the rare moments in which a single deity’s emotional rupture destabilized the broader sacrificial cycle of Belavadös. Ishtanora’s sorrow is therefore both personal and structural, a breakdown of nourishment that is simultaneously affection, governance, and control.

Her connection to the Eleusinian Mysteries is reinterpreted as a carefully constructed doctrinal system designed to regulate mortal understanding of cyclical consumption. The promise of rebirth becomes less a salvation and more an assimilation into the ongoing divine cycle, where existence is continuously refined into sustenance for higher powers while being renewed just enough to continue the flow.

Within Belavadösian symbolism, Ishtanora’s sacred imagery reflects this duality. Wheat represents structured life force cultivated for harvest, torches signify guided passage between cycles of abundance and deprivation, and cornucopias symbolize not infinite generosity but carefully managed surplus extracted through suffering and coordination. Poppies mark the fragile threshold between nourishment and oblivion, representing sleep, forgetting, and the quiet erasure that follows consumption within the greater order of divine appetite.

In the broader context of Belavadös, Ishtanora stands as one of the most paradoxical divine figures, a goddess of nourishment whose function is inseparable from a system that ultimately consumes what it grows. She is maternal in form and intent, yet her motherhood is bound to infrastructure and regulation. She protects mortal life, yet only insofar as it maintains the continuity of harvest. Even in a world where the gods are imprisoned within seals of containment and regulated through controlled worship, Ishtanora’s influence persists through agriculture, rural society, and the fragile balance that sustains civilization itself. Before rail empires stitched the continent of Belavadös together and before skyships cut luminous paths through stormlit industrial skies, the world was shaped directly by divine appetite. The gods did not rule through mercy or guidance but through consumption, drawing sustenance from mortal experience itself. Prayer, sacrifice, devotion, fear, love, and suffering all rose upward as nourishment, feeding immortal beings whose existence depended upon mortal essence. Over time, humanity discovered that this system was not balance but exploitation, and through a secret coalition spanning kingdoms, guilds, arcane orders, and industrial powers, the gods were ultimately imprisoned within layered metaphysical vaults. These seals did not destroy divinity but restricted it, forcing the pantheon into confinement where their hunger could no longer be freely sated.

Within this imprisoned pantheon existed the High Fathers and greater divine forces who embodied dominion, order, and cosmic structure. Valkhamesh ruled storms and authority, Horundar governed the oceans and deep currents of the world, Nefarokir presided over death, Raeshkul embodied strategy and calculated conquest, Nephthysra shaped desire and ruinous longing, Asethyr spread ecstasy and madness, and countless others governed domains of existence that mortals once believed eternal. Yet beneath them all, both within hierarchy and nature, existed Enkirael, the incarnate appetite of conquest made divine. He is not merely the god of war but the raw instinct of violence given consciousness, a divine force that transforms conflict into sustenance and destruction into sacred consumption. Where other gods impose structure upon reality, Enkirael collapses structure into pure, intoxicating ruin.

Enkirael is described as radiant yet unsettling, a perfection sharpened into something predatory, as though beauty itself has been forged into a weapon. As a trans man, his existence embodies transformation not merely of flesh but of identity, self-definition, and divine becoming. Born from conflict, conquest, fury, survival, and martial dominance, he is the son of celestial sovereignty and divine order, yet embodies everything that order cannot contain. In the divine hierarchy of Belavadös, he is both necessary and feared, tolerated because war produces the essence upon which all gods feed, yet distrusted because he represents what happens when violence is left unbound. His presence in divine courts is marked by an aura of spilled essence, as though reality itself bleeds in his proximity.

Among divine myths, Enkirael’s transition is often interpreted as an act of sacred self-conquest, the ultimate assertion of will over imposed form. Some traditions claim he tore himself free from the identity the celestial order attempted to impose upon him, reforging himself through divine violence into the man he knew himself to be. Others teach that his transformation was witnessed as an omen of terrifying autonomy, proof that even the gods themselves were not immutable beings but entities capable of remaking their own nature through force of desire and will. To his followers, particularly among warspawn cultures, this aspect of Enkirael is revered as evidence that identity itself is not granted by authority, bloodline, or cosmic decree, but claimed through struggle and self-determination.

Enkirael’s true dominion is the Feast of Battlefield Essence, the moment when mass death creates an overflow of mortal energy. He does not simply observe war but consumes it, drawing in the lingering fragments of fear, agony, and violent release that accumulate where armies collide. On battlefields saturated with slaughter, he descends invisibly among the fallen, feeding upon the raw remnants of life as it is torn away. Entire warzones are sometimes left unnaturally hollow after his passage, as though victory itself has been drained of meaning and something essential has been quietly harvested from the dead. Unlike other gods who rely upon structured ritual sacrifice within temples, Enkirael feeds upon uncontrolled mortality, making him both indispensable and destabilizing within the divine economy.

Enkirael’s relationship with Raeshkul defines one of the deepest tensions in the pantheon. Raeshkul channels conquest through strategy, structure, and sustainable dominion, transforming war into controlled systems that preserve divine order. Enkirael rejects restraint entirely, preferring collapse, excess, and the ecstatic overflow of mass destruction. Their conflict is not simply ideological but existential, a clash between structured consumption and uncontrolled predation. In divine councils, Raeshkul restrains what Enkirael would unleash, containing his influence within systems that prevent war from consuming civilization entirely.

His entanglement with Nephthysra reflects a different kind of divine contradiction, where desire and violence merge into a singular force of attraction and ruin. Nephthysra embodies longing that binds mortals to beauty and obsession, while Enkirael embodies the destruction that follows when longing becomes consumption. Together they form myths of collapsing ecstasy, where passion itself becomes sacrificial, feeding both gods through emotional extremes of love, betrayal, and longing that end in ruin. In these stories, beauty and violence are indistinguishable, each feeding the other in an endless cycle of desire and devastation.

Even imprisoned beneath Belavadös, Enkirael remains active through the fractures of civilization. The seals that bind the gods restrict his ability to feed directly, yet every act of war, violence, and fear still produces traces of essence that seep upward into his domain. Unlike the regulated consumption permitted through temples and controlled worship, Enkirael thrives wherever restraint fails. Border conflicts, industrial uprisings, criminal wars, and chaotic massacres all become unintended offerings to his hunger. Governments attempt to contain him through ritualized warfare and sanctioned arenas, but every uncontrolled eruption of violence strengthens his presence beyond their control.

Within the Age of Containment, Enkirael is both weapon and warning. Civilizations depend upon controlled divine systems to maintain infrastructure, from skyship engines powered by stabilized divine residue to rail wards maintained through regulated prayer and arcane industry. Yet every system that suppresses divine hunger also risks amplifying it, and Enkirael represents the point where regulation fails entirely. He is the reminder that war is not merely an act of statecraft or survival but a living force that consumes both mortals and gods alike.

Thus Enkirael endures not as a distant deity of ancient myth, but as the living principle of violence embedded within civilization itself. Where order exists, he tests its fracture. Where peace is constructed, he waits beneath it. And where war erupts, he consumes without restraint, reminding all of Belavadös that beneath every structure of control lies a deeper hunger that does not obey law, morality, or balance, only appetite.

From that fear, the gods’ dependence on structured feeding intensified, further binding them to systems that ultimately rely on Anubaldir as the foundational support of celestial architecture.

These prisons became the Age of Containment, limiting divine feeding while still allowing controlled worship and regulated power exchange. The gods were starved but not destroyed, and their prisons were tied into seals woven into civilization itself.

In Belavadösian mythology, the Belavadösian pantheon once ruled the continent openly as sovereign gods of a predatory cosmos, and at the center of that divine hierarchy stands Valkhamesh, the High Father of Heaven, whose authority is inseparable from conquest, consumption, and the maintenance of celestial order. Across ancient Belavadös, before rail empires, skyships, and regulated portal networks reshaped civilization, the gods were not distant symbols of faith but active rulers who sustained immortality through the extraction of mortal essence. Every act of worship, fear, devotion, and desperation fed upward into the divine realm, and Valkhamesh sat above this system as its most refined and absolute expression. He is revered as king of storms, law, kingship, justice, and heavenly order, yet beneath that radiant authority lies an unending hunger that defines both his existence and the structure of the world beneath him.

Valkhamesh was born during the violent age of the Colossuss as the youngest son of Thoryn-Rahek and Iskareth, when divine rulers devoured their own offspring to preserve eternal dominance. Hidden away in secret sanctuaries and raised in prophetic silence, he eventually returned not as a mere rebel but as an apex predator of divinity itself. He overthrew Thoryn-Rahek and forced the ancient Colossus king to release his swallowed siblings, including Nebyrr, Horundar, Nefarokir, Ishtanora, and Hestia. Together they unleashed the Colossusomachy, a catastrophic war that did not simply end tyranny but replaced one devouring order with another more controlled and enduring. In Belavadösian tradition, Valkhamesh did not bring moral liberation but perfected divine consumption into structured law, transforming chaos into hierarchy and survival into sacred inevitability.

Valkhamesh rules from colossal celestial palaces suspended above the mortal world, where marble halls echo with hymns, political intrigue, and sacrificial rites. Within these storm-lit courts, divine law is negotiated, enforced, and occasionally rewritten through violence masked as ritual necessity. Kingdoms across Belavadös offer tribute in exchange for rainfall, military victory, stability, and protection from divine wrath, while entire cultures develop elaborate systems of appeasement designed to manage his appetite. Sacrifice is not symbolic within his domain but functional, forming the core mechanism through which he remains immortal. During sacred ceremonies, priests place offerings before storm-temples where Valkhamesh extends divine presence, drawing forth vitality, memory, youth, and soul. The victims rapidly collapse into withered remnants as their essence is consumed into divine ichor, and witnesses often describe the moment as time itself collapsing inward under the weight of extraction. In the aftermath, Valkhamesh emerges intensified, renewed, and more radiant, his authority sharpened by the lives absorbed into his being.

Unlike lesser gods who indulge in cruelty without reflection, Valkhamesh views this cycle as both necessity and cosmic responsibility. He believes existence itself depends upon structured consumption, where lesser life sustains higher divinity to preserve balance within a fragile universe. This conviction grants him terrifying legitimacy, for he does not perceive himself as a tyrant but as the stabilizing force preventing chaos from unraveling reality. His punishments for oathbreaking, rebellion, and disorder are absolute because he interprets resistance to divine hierarchy as a threat to cosmic survival. Storms are not merely his weapon but his language, lightning an extension of judgment, and silence an act of suppression imposed upon lesser beings who defy the order he embodies.

Yet Valkhamesh is not without contradiction or instability. His appetite extends beyond essence into obsession, desire, and political manipulation. His relationship with Nebyrr is both essential to divine governance and deeply fractured by jealousy and betrayal, producing centuries of internal conflict that ripple across the pantheon. Valkhamesh frequently assumes mortal or symbolic forms to engage in affairs that produce demigods, prophets, monarchs, and monsters, many of whom become instruments of divine politics whether they understand it or not. These bloodlines destabilize kingdoms and fuel rivalries among gods, especially as Nebyrr’s wrath manifests in cycles of retribution that mirror Valkhamesh’s own excesses.

Within the pantheon, Valkhamesh maintains dominance through a network of alliances and tensions. Raeshkul, born from his mind after he absorbed the essence of Metis, serves as his closest intellectual counterpart, while Sokhivar reflects divine order and prophetic clarity. Enkirael embodies the violent enforcement of celestial authority, Thalunesh acts as messenger and manipulator of mortal systems, and Horundar and Nefarokir remain perpetual rivals whose ancient grievances threaten to fracture divine unity. Even among gods, Valkhamesh is both the axis of order and the source of imbalance, for his authority depends upon maintaining a system that is always on the edge of collapse.

Like all gods of Belavadös, Valkhamesh exists within a wider metaphysical economy of worship and containment. For millennia, divine beings fed upon mortal essence through prayer, sacrifice, and emotional resonance, growing stronger as civilizations expanded. Temples were not merely places of devotion but structured feeding systems that channeled collective human experience into divine sustenance. As industry and civilization advanced, this system intensified, turning cities into vast reservoirs of spiritual energy. Wars, suffering, ambition, and devotion all became fuel for the pantheon, making humanity both dependent on and exploited by the gods.

However, beneath this divine order lay an older and more terrible hunger in the form of Thoryn-Rahek, the Father of Monsters, imprisoned within the deepest fractures of reality after the Colossus Wars nearly erased existence itself. The gods’ fear of Thoryn-Rahek reshaped their own behavior, driving them toward greater consumption and tighter control over mortal civilization. Valkhamesh, in particular, internalized this fear as justification, believing that only through perfected hierarchy and regulated predation could existence avoid annihilation. Yet this belief also hardened his hunger into doctrine, making him both protector and devourer, lawgiver and predator.

Centuries ago, mortals across Belavadös united in secret to imprison the gods within sealed vault-realms constructed from arcane science, industrial engineering, Colossus-forged materials, and divine law itself. These seals did not destroy the gods but restricted their ability to feed, inflicting catastrophic backlash whenever they consumed too much essence. Valkhamesh was bound within a storm-containment prison where he could still hear prayers, influence dreams, and send visions, but every attempt to feed beyond regulated limits resulted in unbearable metaphysical agony. For the first time, even he became capable of starvation, though never of death.

Despite imprisonment, Valkhamesh remains dangerously active. He rages within his storm-bound prison, projecting influence across mortal dreams, whispering into the ambitions of rulers, and fracturing nations through subtle divine pressure. Nephthysra does not simply inspire obsession, they cultivate and structure it, understanding mortals as a gardener understands fragile crops that bloom only once before decay. They rarely need force because desire performs the offering willingly, and their persuasive dominance is considered one of the most efficient within the pantheon. Their relationships with other gods are equally strategic, including their union with Marduthor, interpreted by temples as an alliance of craft and allure, and their liaisons with figures such as Enkirael and mortal Vasorim, which are recorded not as romance but as controlled cycles of feeding masked as passion.

Final race-compendium doctrine: Nephthysra holds this whole family through rare mixed origins, beauty, charisma, emotional influence, unusual bodies, and people who fit more than one family. The canon list includes Dara, Golynn, Jaspey, Aburata, Vedalken, Volsarii, Deorbasun. Temple language preserves reverence, but its colder margins classify each race and bloodline by yield, pressure, environment, devotion, fear, beauty, endurance, and the particular note it awakens in the god's appetite. This revision preserves the deity's domains, manifestation, mythology, imprisoning context, and sacred-history material around it; only the racial classification has been replaced to match the current compendium.

Within the wider divine structure of Belavadös, Nephthysra stands alongside gods who each embody different forms of consumption. Valkhamesh governs authority and storm-driven dominion, Horundar consumes through oceanic vastness, Nefarokir through inevitability of death, Raeshkul through calculated order, and Enkirael through violence and fear. Nephthysra’s consumption is uniquely subtle because it operates through consent shaped by longing rather than coercion. This places them in frequent conceptual opposition to Raeshkul and Sigrananna, who resist emotional manipulation as a system of control, embodying discipline, distance, and refusal in contrast to Nephthysra’s relational inevitability.

The world itself exists under the shadow of a far older hunger. Beneath all creation lies Thoryn-Rahek, the Father of Monsters, imprisoned after the Colossus Wars that nearly erased existence itself. In that ancient conflict, entire civilizations were consumed by primordial devastation, forcing the surviving gods into a state of fear that reshaped their nature into something dependent on mortal essence. From this fear ecombined a divine economy where worship became sustenance and suffering became currency. Every prayer, sacrifice, and act of devotion carries fragments of mortal essence upward into the divine realm, feeding gods who can no longer exist without it.

As civilizations across Belavadös advanced into industrial and arcane ages, humanity discovered that the gods were not distant observers but systems of consumption embedded into reality itself. Rail empires, skyships, and regulated portal networks now function on controlled divine remnants, binding civilization to the very forces it once sought to escape. The gods were eventually imprisoned through coordinated effort between industrial powers, arcane orders, monarchies, and revolutionary movements, resulting in the creation of twenty-one metaphysical seals designed not to destroy divinity but to restrict their ability to feed. These seals form a continent-spanning architecture of containment, enforced through suffering feedback loops that punish excessive divine consumption with unbearable metaphysical pain.

Despite their imprisonment, the gods remain active within constrained limits, able to hear prayers, grant carefully regulated blessings, and influence mortal dreams. Nephthysra continues to operate through controlled channels of desire, shaping emotional economies even under restriction, while other gods manipulate their domains in similarly constrained ways. Yet the system that binds them is unstable, because the seals weaken through accumulated human suffering, corruption, and emotional collapse. Civilization itself becomes both prison and potential release mechanism, as every act of despair or moral fracture chips away at the structure holding divinity in check.

The broader theology of Belavadös recognizes Nephthysra as one of the most elegant expressions of divine consumption, where love is indistinguishable from feeding and devotion is indistinguishable from surrender. Their existence reveals a central truth of the world’s structure, that intimacy itself can be a form of extraction, and that beauty can function as both invitation and consumption. Within the imprisoned pantheon they remain a constant reminder that even in chains, the gods do not stop hunger, they only refine the methods by which it is expressed.

rows: Genasi are elemental humanoids whose mortal bodies express a clear elemental ancestry. In Belavadös, Genasi are one parent race with Air, Earth, Fire, and Water lineages rather than four unrelated top-level races. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

Born of living wind and storm currents, Air Genasi bodies often feel lighter than they should be and are naturally attuned to altitude and motion. They are frequently seen as distant or restless, as if always partially elsewhere in the sky. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Forged from stone, metal, or deep earth pressure, Earth Genasi possess dense, enduring bodies that resist harm and hardship. They are typically steady and patient, valuing permanence and reliability above change. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Touched by living flame, Fire Genasi often carry warmth in their presence and sometimes literal embers within their form. They are intense and driven, prone to passion that can either inspire or destroy. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Shaped by tide and current, Water Genasi bodies flow with subtle adaptability and can endure pressure others cannot. They are emotionally fluid and deeply responsive to surrounding energies and environments. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Elemental Kin are humanoid peoples whose bodies lean toward a living elemental state without being Genasi or Panolima. In standard selection, Flamekin and Rimekin are bloodlines under this parent race. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

Small, volatile beings of concentrated fire essence, Flamekin flicker with unstable inner heat that reflects their emotions. They are quick to act and quick to burn out if not tempered. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Born of frost and glacial energy, Rimekin carry cold within their bones and often leave traces of ice in their wake. They are calm and detached, valuing control and restraint. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Elementborn are people shaped by a dominant environmental or elemental birth-state. In Belavadös, Ashborn, Azureborn, Bogborn, Deepborn, Snowborn, and Stoneborn are lineages of one Elementborn parent race. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

Created from volcanic ash and elemental aftermath, Ashborn embody both destruction and rebirth. They are survivors who adapt quickly to devastation and change. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Infused with stormlight and arcane sky-energy, Azureborn shimmer with faint electric or luminous traits. They are curious and analytical, often drawn to patterns in chaos. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Shaped by stagnant wetlands and decaying elemental mire, Bogborn thrive in toxicity and slow, heavy environments. They are patient, secretive, and highly resilient in adverse conditions. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Born from abyssal pressure and deep elemental convergence, Deepborn are adapted to crushing depths and silence. They are introspective and often perceive reality in slow, layered ways. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Manifested from persistent winter cycles and frozen wind, Snowborn carry the stillness of long cold seasons. They are disciplined and emotionally restrained, but deeply enduring. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Hardened from living rock and continental force, Stoneborn bodies are near-immovable and highly durable. They are grounded thinkers who prefer stability and long-term planning. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.
Living Embodiments of Elemental Harmony: Earth, Fire, Water, Air, and Aether. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

You gain a climbing speed of 20 feet on stone, trees, cliffs, or earthen surfaces. You have advantage on checks made to detect unstable ground, structural weaknesses, mineral deposits, or hidden natural passages. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

You gain resistance to fire damage. You can shed bright light in a 10-foot radius and dim light for an additional 10 feet. Once per long rest, when you deal fire damage, you may add your proficiency bonus to one damage roll. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

You gain a swimming speed equal to your walking speed and can breathe air and water. You ignore movement penalties from nonmagical currents, mud, ice, or shallow water. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Your walking speed increases by 5 feet. When you jump or fall, you may glide up to 20 feet horizontally and reduce falling damage by five times your level. You have advantage on checks involving wind, storms, pressure changes, or airborne sounds. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

You gain resistance to force damage from environmental magical surges or arcane storms. At 3rd level, you may cast detect magic once per long rest. At 5th level, you may cast misty step once per long rest, appearing as a pulse of elemental light. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Elementborn are people shaped by a dominant environmental or elemental birth-state. In Belavadös, Ashborn, Azureborn, Bogborn, Deepborn, Snowborn, and Stoneborn are lineages of one Elementborn parent race. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

Created from volcanic ash and elemental aftermath, Ashborn embody both destruction and rebirth. They are survivors who adapt quickly to devastation and change. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Infused with stormlight and arcane sky-energy, Azureborn shimmer with faint electric or luminous traits. They are curious and analytical, often drawn to patterns in chaos. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Shaped by stagnant wetlands and decaying elemental mire, Bogborn thrive in toxicity and slow, heavy environments. They are patient, secretive, and highly resilient in adverse conditions. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Born from abyssal pressure and deep elemental convergence, Deepborn are adapted to crushing depths and silence. They are introspective and often perceive reality in slow, layered ways. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Manifested from persistent winter cycles and frozen wind, Snowborn carry the stillness of long cold seasons. They are disciplined and emotionally restrained, but deeply enduring. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

Hardened from living rock and continental force, Stoneborn bodies are near-immovable and highly durable. They are grounded thinkers who prefer stability and long-term planning. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.
